An Overview of Ecology

  • Ecology is the scientific study of the interactions between organisms and their environments.
    • Valuable insight can be gained from a discovery-based approach of watching nature and recording its structure and processes.
    • Hypothesis-driven science performed in natural environments is fundamental to ecology. But ecologists also test hypotheses using laboratory experiments, where conditions can be simplified and controlled.
    • Some ecologists take a theoretical approach, devising mathematical and computer models.
Text description of this image

A photo shows a biologist wearing a hardhat and collecting vegetation samples on a canvas while hanging from a harness high in the rainforest canopy. Densely forested mountains are seen in the background.

Ecology and Environmentalism

  • Technological innovations have enabled people to colonize just about every environment on Earth.
    • But our survival depends on Earth’s resources, which have been profoundly altered by human activities.
    • Environmental problems can be understood by the science of ecology and require decisions based on values and ethics.

A Hierarchy of Interactions

  • Many different factors can potentially affect an organism’s interaction with the environment.
    • Biotic factors are all the organisms in the area and the living component of the environment.
    • Abiotic factors are the environment’s nonliving component and include chemical and physical factors, such as temperature, light, water, minerals, and air.
    • An organism’s habitat is the specific environment it lives in and includes the biotic and abiotic factors of its surroundings.

Ecology can be divided into four increasingly comprehensive levels.

Energy Source

  • Life depends on pathways that transform energy and matter. All organisms require a usable source of energy to live.
    • Solar energy from sunlight is captured by chlorophyll during the process of photosynthesis and powers most ecosystems.
    • Lack of sunlight is seldom the most important factor limiting plant growth for terrestrial ecosystems, although shading by trees does create intense competition for light among plants growing on forest floors.
  • Life depends on pathways that transform energy and matter. All organisms require a usable source of energy to live.
  • Solar energy from sunlight is captured by chlorophyll during the process of photosynthesis and powers most ecosystems.
  • Lack of sunlight is seldom the most important factor limiting plant growth for terrestrial ecosystems, although shading by trees does create intense competition for light among plants growing on forest floors.

Temperature

  • Temperature is an important abiotic factor because of its effect on metabolism.
    • Few organisms can maintain a sufficiently active metabolism at temperatures close to 0°C.
    • Temperatures above 45°C destroy the enzymes of most organisms.
  • Most organisms function best within a specific range of environmental temperatures.

Water

  • Water is essential to all life.
    • Aquatic organisms are surrounded by water and face problems of water balance if their solute concentration does not match their surroundings.
    • For terrestrial organisms, the primary threat is drying out in the air.
      • Many land animals have watertight coverings that reduce water loss. For example, scales in reptiles, such as snakes and lizards, are structures that perform the function of sealing in moisture.
      • Most plants have waxy coatings on their leaves and other aerial parts.
Text description of this image

Figure A shows scales on a Carolina anole lizard, which fit together tightly. Figure B shows a leaf with beaded water droplets showing the water repellency of the leaf’s waxy coating.

Inorganic Nutrients

  • The distribution and abundance of photosynthetic organisms depend on the availability of inorganic nutrients such as compounds of nitrogen and phosphorus.
  • Soil structure, pH, and nutrient content often play major roles in determining the distribution of plants.
  • In many aquatic ecosystems, low levels of nitrogen and phosphorus limit the growth of algae and photosynthetic bacteria.

Adjusting to Environmental Variability

  • The abiotic factors in a habitat may vary from year to year, seasonally, or over the course of a day.
    • An individual’s abilities to adjust to environmental changes that occur during its lifetime are themselves adaptations refined by natural selection.
    • Birds may adjust to cold by migrating to warmer regions (a behavioral response), grow heavier feathers (an anatomical response), or fluff up their feathers to trap more heat (a physiological response). But these responses, which occur during the lifetime of an individual, do not qualify as evolution, which is change in a population over time.

Physiological Responses

  • Acclimation is a gradual, reversible, physiological adjustment that occurs in response to an environmental change.
    • The ability to acclimate is generally related to the range of environmental conditions a species naturally experiences.
    • Among vertebrates, birds and mammals can generally tolerate the greatest temperature extremes because they are endotherms.
    • Ectothermic reptiles can tolerate only a more limited range of temperatures.

Anatomical Responses

  • Many organisms respond to environmental challenges with some type of change in body shape and structure.
    • When the change is reversible, such as thicker fur coats in winter, the response is an example of acclimation.
    • Other anatomical changes are irreversible over the lifetime of an individual. Environmental variation can affect growth and development so much that there may be remarkable differences in body shape within a population, such as the “flagging” that wind causes in certain trees.

Biomes

  • A biome is a major terrestrial or aquatic life zone, characterized by vegetation type in terrestrial biomes or the physical environment in aquatic biomes.
  • Aquatic biomes occupy roughly 75% of Earth’s surface and are determined by their salinity and other physical factors.
    • Freshwater biomes have a salt concentration of less than 1%.
    • Marine biomes typically have a salt concentration around 3%.

Lakes and Ponds

  • Standing bodies of water range from small ponds to large lakes, such as North America’s Great Lakes.
    • In lakes and large ponds, communities of plants, algae, and animals are distributed according to the depth of water and distance from shore.
    • The photic zone, named because light is available for photosynthesis, includes the shallow water near shore and the upper layer of water away from shore.
    • The aphotic zone is deeper and has light levels too low to support photosynthesis.
    • The benthic realm is at the bottom of all aquatic biomes. It is made up of sand and organic and inorganic sediments, and is occupied by organisms that may include algae, aquatic plants, worms, insect larvae, molluscs, and microorganisms.
    • Phytoplankton is the collective name for microscopic algae and cyanobacteria that drift near the surfaces of aquatic biomes. The amount of phytoplankton growth in a lake or pond is typically regulated by the nutrients nitrogen and phosphorus.
Text description of this image

The figure shows the photic zone, a thin layer of water at the lake’s surface; the thicker aphotic zone below (only away from shore where the water is deeper); and the benthic realm along the bottom of the lake (includes shallow and deep lake bottoms). There is no aphotic zone in the shallow area near shore, as where it is shallow, the photic zone reaches to the lake’s bottom and vegetation grows. In the benthic realm of the aphotic zone, no plants grow.

Rivers and Streams

  • Rivers and streams are bodies of flowing water and generally support quite different communities of organisms than lakes and ponds.
  • A river or stream changes greatly between its source (perhaps a spring or snowmelt in the mountains) and the point at which it empties into a lake or the ocean. Near the source of a stream, the water is usually cold, low in nutrients, and clear. Downstream, the water is usually warmer, murkier, wider, and slower.

Wetlands

  • A wetland is a transitional biome between an aquatic ecosystem and a terrestrial one.
    • Covered with water either permanently or periodically, wetlands support the growth of aquatic plants and are rich in species diversity.
    • Migrating waterfowl and many other birds depend on wetland “pit stops” for food and shelter during their journeys.
    • Wetlands provide water storage areas that reduce flooding and improve water quality by trapping pollutants in their sediments.
Text description of this image

A photo shows a small body of water with lily pads and algae growing on its surface and cattails growing near shore. Larger plant life is visible in the background.

Marine Biomes

Marine biomes are diverse, ranging from vivid coral reefs nearer the surface and dependent on sunlight to perpetually dark realms in the deepest regions.

  • The pelagic realm includes all the open water of the oceans. As in freshwater biomes, the seafloor is known as the benthic realm.
  • In sunlit areas, photosynthesis by phytoplankton and multicellular algae provides energy for a diverse community of animals.
  • Zooplankton (free-floating animals, including many microscopic ones) are abundant in the pelagic photic zone.

  • The coral reef biome occurs in the photic zone of warm tropical waters in scattered locations around the globe.
    • A coral reef is built up slowly by successive generations of coral animals—a diverse group of cnidarians that secrete a hard external skeleton—and by multicellular algae encrusted with limestone.
    • The physical structure and productivity of coral reefs support a huge variety of invertebrates and fishes.

How Climate Affects Terrestrial Biome Distribution

  • Terrestrial biomes are primarily determined by climate, especially temperature and rainfall.
  • Earth’s global climate patterns are largely the result of the input of solar energy and the planet’s movement in space.
    • The equator receives the greatest intensity of solar radiation. Warm, moist air at the equator rises, then cools, forming clouds, and rain falls.
    • This largely explains why rain forests are concentrated in the tropics, the region from the Tropic of Cancer to the Tropic of Capricorn.

How Uneven Heating of Earth Produces Various Climates

Text description of this image

The figure shows half of the globe being struck by sunlight at different latitudes. At high latitudes such as 60 degrees North (near the Arctic Circle) and South (near the Antarctic Circle) the curvature of the Earth means that there is a low angle of incoming sunlight. The sunlight spreads out over a diffuse area (and is less intense). The angle of sunlight becomes more direct (concentrated on a smaller area) toward the Tropic of Cancer (north of the equator) and the Tropic of Capricorn (south of the equator). Sunlight strikes most directly (and is most intense) at the equator (0 degrees). The drawing of the Earth in the diagram shows that the middle of the African continent is green and passes through the equator, while Northern Africa is desert and extends to about 30 degrees North.

Text description of this image

The figure shows that in the tropics, sunlight strikes most directly at 0 degree (doldrums), resulting in ascending moist air that releases moisture (rain). Trade winds blow the air masses away from the equator. The air dries as it passes 23.5 degrees on both sides of the equator and crosses into Temperate Zones. As the air dries and cools, it descends at 30 degree North and South. Descending dry air absorbs moisture. Some air then continues toward the poles while some circulates back toward the equator, becoming moist again as it passes the tropics, warms, and rises.

How Climate Affects Terrestrial Biome Distribution

  • Climate is also affected by proximity to large bodies of water and the presence of landforms such as mountain ranges.
  • Mountains affect climate in two major ways.
    1. Air temperature drops as elevation increases. As a result, driving up a tall mountain offers a quick tour of several biomes.
    2. Mountains can block the flow of cool, moist air from a coast and cause radically different climates on opposite sides of a mountain range.

How Mountains Affect Rainfall

Text description of this image

The figure shows the Pacific Ocean, Coast Range, Sierra Nevada, and desert to the east of the Sierra. The coast range is a low mountain range, while the Sierra is much higher. Moist air from over the Pacific Ocean blows toward land and travels up and over the small Coast Range. As the air rises and cools it rains, making the Coast Range and inland valley green. Air continues to flow inland until it hits the tall Sierra Nevada mountains, where it is forced up and over the high mountain peaks. Because the mountains are high, the air cools as it rises over them, and rain falls on the windward (Pacific) side of the Sierra (with snow falling on the high peaks). The air that travels over the back of the Sierra and descends to the eastern side is therefore dry, forming a rain shadow (desert) on the east (leeward) side of the Sierra.

Terrestrial Biomes

  • Terrestrial ecosystems are grouped into biomes primarily based on their vegetation type.
    • The geographic distribution of plants, and thus of biomes, largely depends on climate, with temperature and rainfall often the key factors determining the kind of biome in a particular region.
    • If the climate in two geographically separate areas is similar, they may have the same type of biome.
    • Organisms in widely separated biomes may look alike because of convergent evolution, the appearance of similar traits in independently evolved species living in similar environments.

A Map of the Major Terrestrial Biomes

Text description of this image

The map shows the following:

Tropical forest: Found between the Tropics of Cancer north of the equator and Capricorn south of the equator in Central America, tropical South America, central Africa, India and Southeast Asia, tropical Pacific Islands, and tropical Australia.; Savanna: Found in a small strips bordering tropical forest in northern and eastern South America, Africa, Central Asia, and Australia.; Desert: Mostly found at 30 degrees North and South in North and South America, in Africa, Asia and Australia.; Chaparral: Found in small regions along the west coast of North America, both southern coasts of South America, on the southern coast of Australia, at the tip of South Africa, and around the Mediterranean.; Temperate grassland: A large patch and a few smaller patches in central North America, on the east coast of South America, in large swaths surrounding desert in Asia, and in a small patch near the tip of South Africa.; Temperate broadleaf forest: Found in a large section of eastern North America, in Europe, along the east coasts of Asia and Australia, and in New Zealand.

Northern coniferous forest: Found just below Tundra in a thick band across northern North America, northern Europe, and Russia.

Tundra: Thin band bordering Northern Coniferous Forest to the north; also found on the northern islands.; High mountains (coniferous forest and alpine tundra): Found in thin strips running along the west coasts of North and South America; in a small band at the equator in central Africa; a small patch in Europe; and a larger band bordering desert and tropical forest in Asia.; Polar ice: Found at Greenland and the poles.

The Water Cycle

  • All parts of the biosphere are linked by the global water cycle and nutrient cycles.
    • Water and air move in global patterns driven by solar energy.
    • On land, precipitation exceeds evaporation and transpiration. The excess precipitation may stay on the surface, or it may trickle through the soil to become groundwater.

The Global Water Cycle

Text description of this image

The figure shows that global water cycle is powered by solar heat from the sun. Over the ocean, evaporation is greater than precipitation, so more water moves into water vapor over the sea (as clouds) than falls as rain back to the ocean. There is a net onshore movement of water vapor by wind. Over the land, precipitation is greater than evaporation and transpiration, so more water falls from clouds as rain than evaporates or transpires as water vapor (clouds). Water that falls as rain is stored as surface water (lakes and rivers) and groundwater (stored underground). Because the land slopes toward sea, some surface and groundwater flows back from the land to the sea.

Human Impact on Biomes

  • For hundreds of years, people have been using increasingly effective technologies to capture or produce food, to extract resources from the environment, and to build cities. It is now clear that the environmental costs of these enterprises are staggering.
  • Sustainability is the goal of developing, managing, and conserving Earth’s resources in ways that meet the needs of people today without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their needs.

Fresh Water

  • The impact of human activities on freshwater ecosystems may pose a greater threat to life on Earth than damage to terrestrial ecosystems.
  • Freshwater ecosystems are being polluted by large amounts of nitrogen and phosphorus compounds that run off from heavily fertilized farms.
  • Other pollutants, including industrial wastes, also contaminate freshwater habitats and groundwater.
Text description of this image

A satellite photo shows Las Vegas taken in May 1973 with very less human settlement. Desert and mountains surround the area. Another satellite photo shows Las Vegas taken in October, 2013 with a dramatic expansion of the human presence, with green areas covering approximately six times the area in 2013 as they did in 1973. Desert and mountains surround the area.

Climate Change

Rising concentrations of carbon dioxide (CO2) and certain other gases in the atmosphere are changing global climate patterns.

Text description of this image

A figure illustrates the greenhouse effect. The figure shows that sunlight travels to Earth’s atmosphere, where radiant heat is trapped by greenhouse gasses. Some heat energy escapes into space.

Text description of this image

The figure shows a forest, a farm with livestock, rigs for drilling oil, a road with cars, a power plant, and the ocean. The width of arrows in the diagram indicate the relative contribution of the processes involved in moving carbon in and out of the atmosphere. Over land, photosynthesis moves carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere, but the effect of respiration moving carbon dioxide from living organisms back to the atmosphere is slightly greater due to deforestation. Even greater is the effect of the combustion of fossil fuels (combines the effect of the oil rigs, the cars, and the power plant) in moving carbon dioxide back into the atmosphere. Over the ocean, the effect of photosynthesis pulling carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere is much greater than the effect of respiration sending CO2 back to the atmosphere.
